btos.label: Real estate and rental and leasing (NAICS 53)

name: Real Estate
blurb: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest AI and now federally regulated under FHFA and CFPB quality-control rules; plus valuation, leasing, and property-management platforms with methodology disclosed.

points.desc: Census BTOS reports real-estate sector AI use directly from firms.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The interagency Quality Control Standards for Automated Valuation Models - finalized by FHFA, CFPB, and the banking regulators - are the first binding federal rules for the sector's core AI: the models that value homes in mortgage decisions.
points.name: AVMs are now federally regulated AI

points.desc: The bureau's AVM rule page and its algorithmic-appraisal work are the record of how valuation bias and model accountability are supervised.
points.name: CFPB carries the consumer-protection side

points.desc: The National Association of Realtors' technology research tracks what AI tools agents and brokerages actually adopt.
points.name: NAR surveys the profession

points.desc: The Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation publishes the funding data on AI and proptech startups - the sector's investment barometer.
points.name: CRETI tracks proptech capital

points.desc: The Zestimate and the Redfin Estimate are the consumer-facing AVMs, each with published methodology and error rates - rare public documentation of production ML.
points.name: Zillow and Redfin publish their valuation models

points.desc: The iBuyer's pricing models carry real balance-sheet exposure - its own filings and documentation are the record of valuation AI with capital consequences.
points.name: Opendoor prices houses with models at risk

points.desc: JLL and CBRE - the commercial real estate services majors - deploy generative and predictive AI across brokerage, facilities, and portfolio analytics.
points.name: The CRE giants run enterprise AI

points.desc: 3D capture and computer vision digitizing physical space - the data layer under virtual touring and property intelligence.
points.name: Matterport turns buildings into data

points.desc: EliseAI's leasing agents and AppFolio's property-management AI are where the sector's day-to-day automation ships.
points.name: Leasing and property ops are automating

points.desc: CREtech is the commercial proptech community and event network; MetaProp is the sector's dedicated venture firm publishing funding and sentiment research - together the clearest read on where proptech capital goes.
points.name: CREtech and MetaProp track the proptech market

points.desc: The Building Owners and Managers Association tracks AI in smart-building operations, energy efficiency, and predictive maintenance across commercial property.
points.name: BOMA covers commercial building operations

points.desc: The realtor association's technology accelerator is where residential proptech gets vetted and scaled - a window into which tools the profession is actually adopting.
points.name: NAR REACH backs the startups

points.desc: The residential brokerage's platform applies AI to agent workflows, client matching, and predictive listing recommendations.
points.name: Compass runs AI inside the brokerage workflow

points.desc: HouseCanary's valuation and forecasting models and Cherre's data integration layer are what institutional investors underwrite on - the wholesale side of the AVM story.
points.name: Institutional valuation runs on data platforms

points.desc: Prophia extracts terms, rent rolls, and obligations from commercial leases automatically - one of the clearest production uses of document AI in the sector.
points.name: Lease abstraction is a document-AI problem

points.desc: Visitt and Building Engines apply IoT sensing and machine learning to HVAC optimization, maintenance prediction, and tenant workflow in operating buildings.
points.name: Smart buildings close the operations loop

summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
# Real Estate

According to the U.S. Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.9 percent of real estate and rental and leasing firms reported using AI in the last two weeks, up from 28.0 percent in the prior period. This adoption level masks significant concentration in high-stakes applications. Automated valuation models, or AVMs, have become the regulatory center of gravity for AI in the sector. The Federal Housing Finance Agency and Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, along with the banking regulators, have adopted binding quality control standards for AVMs used by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers to determine collateral value on consumer dwellings, implementing requirements from the Dodd-Frank Act for policies, procedures, and control systems designed to ensure confidence in AVM estimates, protect against data manipulation, and require random sample testing and compliance reviews.

On the residential side, valuation AI is now public-facing and methodologically transparent. Zillow publishes Zestimate valuations for 110 million homes using neural network models that incorporate county records, MLS data, and hundreds of data points per property, with estimated sales ranges reflecting model uncertainty. These models update multiple times per week and have been refined over nearly two decades of research and engineering. Similar platforms like HouseCanary provide valuations and market forecasts for over 136 million U.S. properties, combining curated data from thousands of sources with AI-driven and manual quality control to power decisions by residential investors, agents, and loan officers. The transparency around methodology and error rates in these systems is rare in production machine learning and reflects both the capital sensitivity of valuation and the regulatory environment now governing the field.

Commercial real estate operations and leasing workflows have emerged as the sector's fastest-growing AI deployment ground. Lease abstraction platforms like Prophia use AI to extract key terms and combine extraction with expert validation to produce structured lease data for risk management and decision-making. Conversational AI and agentic automation platforms like EliseAI are handling communications and operational tasks at scale in property management and housing operations, streamlining workflows and reducing overhead by automating responses to leads, residents, and maintenance requests 24/7. Building Engines, a JLL company, operates an AI-powered property management platform that delivers instant answers, recommendations, and automation to help commercial real estate teams move faster and focus on higher-value work. Three-dimensional capture and computer vision through platforms like Matterport digitize buildings into immersive virtual tours and property intelligence data, integrating with construction and facilities management tools to centralize management decisions and reduce site visits.

The vendor landscape is bifurcated between giant enterprises and specialized startups. JLL has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company and deploys it across brokerage, facilities, and portfolio analytics, while Compass operates AI inside residential brokerage workflows for client matching and listing recommendations. The proptech capital ecosystem is tracked by CRETI, the Center for Real Estate Technology and Innovation, and organized around industry events like CREtech New York, where 3,000 leaders and 150 speakers converge to discuss real deployment and strategy. NAR REACH, the National Association of Realtors' technology accelerator program run by Second Century Ventures, serves as a vetted scaling mechanism for residential real estate technology startups.

Risk and regulatory posture center on valuation accuracy and algorithmic accountability. The federal AVM rule mandates quality control standards for models that determine whether consumers qualify for mortgage credit, creating explicit liability for model performance and data integrity. Opendoor, an iBuyer that prices homes with proprietary models, carries its valuation risk directly on the balance sheet, making its model performance a matter of financial results disclosure. The profession has not uniformly adopted regulatory frameworks for document AI, agent-assistance algorithms, or property operations automation beyond the valuation core, leaving substantial portions of proptech deployment outside formal compliance regimes. For organizations evaluating AI deployment in real estate, the evidence points to highest confidence and regulatory maturity in valuation and title-adjacent automation, lower regulatory clarity in agent-workflow and leasing platforms, and emerging but unregulated territory in conversational AI for property operations.
